Yonhap NewsThis week, the government will outline its economic growth strategy for the second half of the year, while the Bank of Korea (BOK) decides on its base rate. Whether employment indicators have recovered is also a focus.Through its second-half economic growth strategy this week, the government will release a revised forecast for this year's economic growth rate. In January, it had projected 2%, but the figure is expected to be sharply raised this time on the back of strong semiconductor exports. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) recently raised their forecasts for Korea's real growth rate this year to as high as 2.6%. The government is also expected to additionally unveil key second-half policies aimed at achieving a major economic leap.The BOK will hold a Monetary Policy Board meeting on the 16th to decide whether to adjust the base rate, currently at 2.5%. Citing the high economic growth rate driven by the semiconductor super cycle, high inflation from the Middle East war, the high exchange rate hovering in the 1,500 won range, and rising housing prices in the greater Seoul area, there is a strong possibility that it will raise the rate by 0.25 percentage points this time. If the rate is raised this time, it will mark the first tightening decision in three years and six months since January 2023. Attention is also focused on what Governor Shin Hyun-song, who has repeatedly stated that he will raise rates at an appropriate time, will say at the press conference immediately following the Monetary Policy Board meeting.Ahead of this, Statistics Korea will release the "June Employment Trends" on the 15th. Previously in May, the number of employed persons aged 15 and over fell by 40,000 from a year earlier, recording a decline for the first time in 17 months since December 2024, when the martial law occurred. As the government is working to increase the number of employed persons through policies such as the Youth New Deal, attention is drawn to whether there will be a change in employment indicators.Overseas, U.S. inflation is the point to watch. The June Consumer Price Index (CPI) will be released, with the market forecasting a 3.8% rise from a year earlier. This is seen as a moderation from May's 4.2% gain. As employment data released earlier came in weaker than the market expected, a slowdown in inflation as well could ease concerns over a rate hike.Kevin Warsh, chairman of the U.S. Federal Reserve (Fed), will appear before Congress for the first time since taking office to report on monetary policy and the economic outlook. With the July Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting just two weeks away, the market's attention is focused on hearing the Fed chairman's position.In addition, the U.S. second-quarter earnings season begins this week, with major U.S. banks and semiconductor companies such as ASML and TSMC releasing their results. China's second-quarter economic growth rate announcement is also scheduled.
